analysis.one_liner: Lets patients see, supplement, and control who sees their medical records, with fines for misuse.
analysis.headline: The Senate health committee never acted on the bill: introduced March 10, 1999 and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, it received no hearing or vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give patients the right to see and copy their own medical records, add corrections, and control who else sees them, including employers and insurers. It would require anyone holding health records — doctors, health plans, employers, insurers, schools, researchers — to safeguard the information, and it would create a federal privacy office inside the Department of Health and Human Services to investigate complaints, with civil penalties and up to 10 years in prison for knowingly selling or misusing medical data. The bill was a response to a 1996 law (HIPAA) that told Congress to pass health privacy legislation by August 1999 [S2]. It never got a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients. The bill would give every patient the right to inspect and copy their own medical records within 15 business days, file supplements to correct the record, and get a written notice of who sees their information [S3]. It would bar employers from using workers' health records in personnel decisions without a separate, explicit authorization, and stop health plans and insurers from conditioning coverage on broad consent to share information [S3]. It would create a dedicated Office of Health Information Privacy to investigate complaints, impose civil fines up to $100,000 for bad practices, and criminal penalties — up to $500,000 and 10 years in prison — for selling or misusing protected health information [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Patients gain enforceable access to their own medical records, with inspection and copying requests honored within 15 business days and fees limited to actual cost.

Employers and health plans could not make coverage or personnel decisions dependent on broad waivers; disclosure for anything other than treatment or payment requires a separate written authorization the patient can revoke.
The bill creates criminal penalties, including up to 10 years' imprisonment and $500,000 in fines for disclosures made for commercial gain, and lets patients sue for damages.
Anyone holding health records must build safeguards — access controls, audit trails, encryption — and keep a record of who accessed electronic files, for at least seven years.

analysis.who_pays: The entities that hold and move health records: hospitals and doctors' offices, health insurers and life insurers, employers, universities, and research institutions, all of which would face compliance costs — authorizations, safeguards, disclosure recordkeeping, staff training. Insurers and employers would also lose a business convenience: the free ability to use patients' health information for purposes beyond treating and paying for care.

drawbacks.text: Compliance would be costly and bureaucratic: every covered provider, plan, employer, and school would need new authorization forms, security systems, disclosure logs kept for seven years, and audits, and smaller providers would feel the burden most.

Critics of strong medical privacy rules argued the requirements could slow care coordination, referrals, and research; the bill tries to manage this by carving out treatment, payment, public health, oversight, and court-ordered law enforcement access, and by leaving research consent rules to a later HHS study rather than mandating them immediately.

The civil penalty schedule is modest by entity-level standards — for example, a single noncompliant practice faces at most $50,000 in aggregate penalties for title II violations unless violations rise to a general business practice, which opponents said was too light to deter large institutions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients the bill offered real, enforceable control over intimate information held by employers, insurers, and others. The main cost is compliance — paperwork, security systems, and slower information flows — which the bill tried to limit through carve-outs for treatment, payment, public health, and court-ordered access, and by deferring the research-consent question to a regulatory study. The tradeoff is genuine, but the bill never got far enough for the debate over those costs to actually happen.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat there until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: HIPAA, passed in 1996, set a deadline for Congress itself to enact comprehensive health privacy legislation before August 21, 1999.
Leahy, Kennedy, Daschle, and Dorgan introduced this bill in March 1999 as that comprehensive answer; it drew seven Democratic cosponsors in total.

On the day of introduction the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; the record shows no hearing, no markup, and no vote for the remainder of the Congress, only additional sponsor remarks in December 2000.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The companies and institutions that hold medical records — health and life insurers, employers, and data handlers — are better off, because they kept using health information without individual consent requirements, federal penalties, or a dedicated enforcement office. Congress also never had to choose between competing privacy bills, so the question was left unsettled for the industry and for patients.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's eight named supporters were all Democrats, but privacy legislation had supporters in both parties at the time, and the bill never reached a vote where any party split would have been recorded.

industries.note: The bill would require signed, revocable authorizations before insurers could use or disclose policyholders' health information, bar conditioning coverage on broad consent, and expose insurers to civil fines and debarment from federal health programs. Insurers' freedom to use medical data for underwriting and other purposes would shrink under rules that run against the public's interest in privacy.

Employers could not disclose workers' health information to anyone making employment or work-assignment decisions without a separate written authorization, ending a common practice of tracking employee health records. The bill's restrictions on employer use of health data align with workers' interest in privacy.

Doctors, hospitals, and clinics would bear the heaviest day-to-day compliance costs — authorizations at intake, security safeguards, and seven-year disclosure logs. But they also keep the disclosure exceptions for treatment, payment, and emergencies, and stronger confidentiality supports patient trust in seeking care.

The bill extends federal human-subjects protections to all health research using identifiable data and directs HHS to study whether written informed consent should be required before records are used for research. Researchers keep access to identifiable data in the interim but face new safeguards, identifier-destruction requirements, and monitoring of review boards.
